title: Unit 1: One World: Countries, Nationalities & To Be
objective: Master The verb 'to be' (am/is/are) - affirmative, negative, questions, short answers, contractions and vocabulary for Countries and nationalities, greetings, identities, capital cities across 4 structured sub-modules

theory.title: Meeting International Students: Countries, Nationalities & The Verb 'To Be'
theory.summary: In this section, you will read about two international students, Mateo and Mei. You will learn vocabulary for countries and nationalities, and study how to use the verb 'to be' (am, is, are) to talk about where people are from.
theory.objective: By the end of this section, you can read a short text about people from different countries, understand key vocabulary for countries and nationalities, and identify correct uses of the verb 'to be' in affirmative sentences.
theory.contextWarmUp: Look at the flags of Spain and China. Can you guess which countries they represent? What languages do people speak there? Where are the capital cities? Think about your answers before you read the passage below.

items.meaning: A country in southern Europe. The capital city is Madrid.
The nationality of a person from Spain.
A large country in East Asia. The capital city is Beijing.
The nationality of a person from China.
The most important city in a country, where the government is.
items.collocation: Madrid is the capital city of Spain.

items.meaning: A person who studies at a school or university.
items.collocation: Mateo is a student at an international school.

readingPassage.title: Two New Friends
paragraphs: Hello! My name is Mateo. I am from Spain. I am Spanish. My capital city is Madrid. I am 15 years old. I am a student at an international school. Nice to meet you!

Hi! My name is Mei. I am from China. I am Chinese. My capital city is Beijing. I am 14 years old. I am a student too. Mateo and I are friends. We are in the same class. We are happy at our new school!
readingPassage.audioText: Hello! My name is Mateo. I am from Spain. I am Spanish. My capital city is Madrid. I am 15 years old. I am a student at an international school. Nice to meet you! Hi! My name is Mei. I am from China. I am Chinese. My capital city is Beijing. I am 14 years old. I am a student too. Mateo and I are friends. We are in the same class. We are happy at our new school!

rules.explanation: When you talk about yourself, always use 'I am' or the contraction 'I'm'. No other subject uses 'am'.
rules.example: I am from Spain. / I'm from Spain.

rules.explanation: For one other person or thing, use 'is'. You can also use contractions: he's, she's, it's.
For 'you' (singular and plural), 'we', and 'they', always use 'are'. Contractions: you're, we're, they're.

postTestQuestions.explanation: Mateo says: 'I am 15 years old.'

postTestQuestions.question: Which sentence uses the verb 'to be' correctly?
postTestQuestions.explanation: The subject 'we' requires the verb 'are'. 'We are friends' is grammatically correct.

postTestQuestions.question: What is the capital city of China according to the passage?
postTestQuestions.explanation: Mei says: 'My capital city is Beijing.'

readingPassage.title: New Students at International School
paragraphs: Hi! My name is Lucas. I am from Brazil. I am Brazilian. The capital city of Brazil is Brasilia. I am 13 years old. I am a new student at the international school. I am not Spanish. I am not Chinese. I am Brazilian! Nice to meet you!

Hello! I am Kenji. I am from Japan. I am Japanese. The capital city of Japan is Tokyo. I am 14 years old. Lucas and I are not from the same country, but we are in the same class. We are friends. We are happy at our school. Are you a new student too?

I am not Spanish. I am not Chinese. I am Brazilian! Nice to meet you! Hello! I am Kenji. I am from Japan. I am Japanese. The capital city of Japan is Tokyo. I am 14 years old. Lucas and I are not from the same country, but we are in the same class. We are friends. We are happy at our school. Are you a new student too?

B) Two new international students introduce themselves.

C) The nationality of a person from Brazil

D) Kenji says they are friends.

theory.title: Listening to an International School Conversation
theory.context: It is the first day at an international school. Mateo from Spain meets Kenji from Japan in the classroom. They introduce themselves and ask about each other's country and nationality.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.en: Hello! My name is Mateo. What is your name?

lines.speaker: Kenji
lines.en: Hi, Mateo! My name is Kenji. Nice to meet you!

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.en: Nice to meet you too, Kenji! Where are you from?

lines.speaker: Kenji
lines.en: I am from Japan. I am Japanese. Where are you from?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.en: I am from Spain. I am Spanish. My capital city is Madrid.

lines.speaker: Kenji
lines.en: That is great! The capital city of Japan is Tokyo. How old are you?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.en: I am 15 years old. How old are you?

lines.speaker: Kenji
lines.en: I am 14 years old. Are you a new student?

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.en: Yes, I am! Are you a new student too?

lines.speaker: Kenji
lines.en: Yes, I am. We are both new students! That is cool!

rules.explanation: When you listen to a conversation, focus on important words like names, countries, nationalities, and numbers (ages). These words carry the main meaning of the dialogue.
rules.example: In the sentence 'I am from Japan', the key information word is 'Japan' because it tells you the country.

rules.explanation: Yes/No questions (like 'Are you Spanish?') have a rising intonation at the end. Wh- questions (like 'Where are you from?') have a falling intonation at the end. Recognizing this helps you understand what type of answer is expected.
rules.example: 'Where are you from?' ends with falling intonation. 'Are you a new student?' ends with rising intonation.

postTestQuestions.explanation: The dialogue begins with Mateo saying: 'Hello! My name is Mateo.'

theory.title: Writing with the Verb 'To Be': Affirmative, Negative & Questions
theory.summary: In this section, you will learn how to write sentences using the verb 'to be' (am, is, are). You will practise affirmative sentences (I am Spanish.), negative sentences (She is not Chinese.), and questions (Are you from Brazil?). You will also learn about contractions (I'm, he's, isn't, aren't) and the rules for capitalizing country names and nationalities.

rules.rule: Affirmative, Negative, and Question Forms of 'To Be'
rules.explanation: Affirmative: Subject + am/is/are + complement. Negative: Subject + am not / is not / are not + complement. Question: Am/Is/Are + subject + complement? Short answers: Yes, I am. / No, he isn't.
rules.example: Affirmative: He is Mexican. Negative: He is not Mexican. (He isn't Mexican.) Question: Is he Mexican? Yes, he is. / No, he isn't.

rules.explanation: In informal writing and speaking, we often shorten the verb 'to be': I am = I'm, you are = you're, he is = he's, she is = she's, it is = it's, we are = we're, they are = they're. Negative contractions: is not = isn't, are not = aren't.
rules.example: I'm from Australia. She isn't Egyptian. They aren't from Russia.

rules.explanation: Country names (Spain, Japan, Brazil) and nationality adjectives (Spanish, Japanese, Brazilian) always start with a capital letter in English. This is a fixed rule.
rules.example: Correct: She is Italian. She is from Italy. Incorrect: she is italian. she is from italy.

postTestQuestions.question: Which sentence is written correctly?
postTestQuestions.explanation: 'I' is always capitalized, and 'Mexico' is a country name so it must start with a capital letter. The sentence also starts with a capital letter.

postTestQuestions.question: What is the correct contraction of 'She is not Australian'?
postTestQuestions.explanation: 'Is not' contracts to 'isn't'. The correct sentence is 'She isn't Australian.'

postTestQuestions.question: Choose the correct question form:
postTestQuestions.explanation: To form a Yes/No question with 'to be', put the verb before the subject: Are + you + from Egypt?

postTestQuestions.question: Which short answer is correct for the question 'Is he Russian?'
postTestQuestions.explanation: The subject 'he' uses the verb 'is'. The correct short answer is 'Yes, he is.'

postTestQuestions.question: Which sentence correctly uses the negative form?
postTestQuestions.explanation: 'They' uses 'are'. The negative contraction is 'aren't'. So: 'They aren't British.'

challenge.scenario: You are a new student at an international school. Write a short self-introduction (3 to 5 sentences). Include your name, your age, your country, and your nationality. Use the verb 'to be' correctly. Example start: 'Hello! My name is...'
rubrics: Grammar accuracy of 'to be': All uses of am/is/are must be correct, including at least one contraction (e.g., I'm).
Proper capitalization and spelling: Country names and nationalities must start with capital letters, and all words must be spelled correctly.

theory.title: Pronunciation Guide: Sounds, Stress & Intonation for Countries and Greetings
theory.summary: In this section, you will practise pronouncing country names and nationalities clearly. You will learn about the /h/ sound in 'Hello' and 'How', the /w/ sound in 'Where' and 'What', syllable stress in words like 'Ja-PAN' and 'Jap-a-NESE', and the difference between rising intonation (for Yes/No questions) and falling intonation (for Wh- questions and statements).

rules.rule: Syllable Stress in Countries and Nationalities
rules.explanation: Every word has one syllable that is louder and longer than the others. For countries: Ja-PAN, Bra-ZIL, E-GYPT. For nationalities: Jap-a-NESE, Bra-ZIL-ian, E-GYP-tian. Stressing the wrong syllable can make the word hard to understand.
rules.example: Say 'Jap-a-NESE' with stress on the third syllable: /ˌdʒæp.əˈniːz/. Say 'SPAN-ish' with stress on the first syllable: /ˈspæn.ɪʃ/.

rules.rule: Rising and Falling Intonation in Questions
rules.explanation: Yes/No questions end with rising intonation (your voice goes up): 'Are you Spanish?' ↗ Wh- questions end with falling intonation (your voice goes down): 'Where are you from?' ↘ Statements also use falling intonation: 'I am from Italy.' ↘
rules.example: Rising: 'Are you from China?' ↗ Falling: 'Where are you from?' ↘

items.meaning: A common greeting used when you meet someone.
A question word used to ask about a place or location.
The nationality of a person from Japan. Stress is on the third syllable.
The nationality of a person from Brazil. Stress is on the second syllable.
The nationality of a person from Egypt. Stress is on the second syllable.
The nationality of a person from Australia. Stress is on the second syllable.

postTestQuestions.question: Which syllable is stressed in the word 'Japanese'?
postTestQuestions.explanation: In 'Japanese' (/ˌdʒæp.əˈniːz/), the primary stress falls on the third syllable: -NESE.

postTestQuestions.question: What type of intonation does the question 'Are you from Mexico?' have?
postTestQuestions.explanation: 'Are you from Mexico?' is a Yes/No question. Yes/No questions end with rising intonation.

postTestQuestions.question: Someone asks you 'Where are you from?' What is the best response?
postTestQuestions.explanation: 'Where are you from?' asks about your country. The correct response states your country: 'I am from Italy.'

postTestQuestions.question: Which word starts with the /w/ sound?
postTestQuestions.explanation: 'Where' starts with the /w/ sound: /weər/. 'Hello', 'How', and 'He' start with the /h/ sound.

postTestQuestions.question: Someone says 'How old are you?' What is the correct response?
postTestQuestions.explanation: 'How old are you?' asks about your age. The correct response includes your age: 'I am 13 years old.'

drills.targetText: Hello! My name is Mateo. I am from Spain.
drills.focus: Practise the /h/ sound in 'Hello' and smooth linking between 'My name is'.
drills.hint: Make sure you breathe out a small puff of air for the /h/ in 'Hello'. Link 'name is' so it sounds like 'name-iz'.

drills.targetText: Where are you from? I am from Japan.
drills.focus: Practise the /w/ sound in 'Where' and falling intonation on the Wh- question.
drills.hint: Round your lips for the /w/ in 'Where'. Let your voice go down at the end of 'Where are you from?'

drills.targetText: Are you Brazilian? No, I am not. I am Mexican.
drills.focus: Practise rising intonation on the Yes/No question and stress on 'Bra-ZIL-ian' and 'MEX-i-can'.
drills.hint: Let your voice rise at the end of 'Are you Brazilian?' Stress the second syllable in 'Brazilian' and the first syllable in 'Mexican'.

drills.targetText: She is Egyptian. She is from Egypt. The capital city is Cairo.
drills.focus: Practise the stress pattern in 'E-GYP-tian' and 'E-GYPT'.
drills.hint: Stress the second syllable: e-GYP-tian /ɪˈdʒɪp.ʃən/. Make sure 'Cairo' is pronounced /ˈkaɪ.rəʊ/.

drills.targetText: Nice to meet you! How old are you? I am 14 years old.
drills.focus: Practise the /h/ in 'How', natural rhythm in 'Nice to meet you', and clear number pronunciation.
drills.hint: Say 'Nice to meet you' as one smooth phrase. Breathe out for /h/ in 'How'. Say 'fourteen' clearly: /fɔːˈtiːn/.

roleplay.context: You are a new student at an international school. Your teacher, Mr. Khoirul, welcomes you on your first day and asks you some questions. Answer using your own information or invented details. Use the verb 'to be' and vocabulary from this unit.

turns.text: Good morning! Welcome to our international school. What is your name?

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: (Say your name. Example: Hello! My name is Ana.)

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: Nice to meet you! Where are you from?

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: (Say your country and nationality. Example: I am from Italy. I am Italian.)

turns.speaker: Mr. Khoirul
turns.text: That is wonderful! How old are you?

turns.speaker: Student
turns.text: (Say your age. Example: I am 13 years old.)

turns.speaker: Student

challenge.scenario: Record a 30-second spoken self-introduction. Say your name, your age, your country, your nationality, and one extra sentence (for example, the capital city of your country). Speak clearly and use correct intonation. Example: 'Hello! My name is Lucas. I am 13 years old. I am from Brazil. I am Brazilian. The capital city of Brazil is Brasilia. Nice to meet you!'
rubrics: Articulation and pronunciation accuracy: All country names, nationalities, and key phrases are pronounced clearly with correct syllable stress.
Conversational fluency and response speed: The introduction flows naturally without long pauses, and intonation patterns (rising for questions, falling for statements) are used appropriately.
